unverified.claim: National-symbol status after 2023

unverified.claim: IUCN Red List pages themselves
unverified.reason: iucnredlist.org blocks automated fetching; categories, years, assessors and DOIs were taken from GBIF's mirror of the IUCN assessments and the DOI strings are recorded as iucn.url.

unverified.claim: Simplified Chinese common names (凤尾绿咬鹃, 中美貘, 白尾鹿, 大蓝鹭, 火山蜂鸟, 紫喉宝石蜂鸟)
unverified.reason: Supplied from general knowledge; no zh page was fetched within the budget. The two hummingbird names are literal renderings. Recorded with status uncertain.

unverified.claim: Which Spanish common names Costa Ricans actually use for the quetzal, the heron and the two hummingbirds
unverified.reason: Spanish Wikipedia lists several names for each species without attributing them to countries, except 'chispita volcanera' (Costa Rica) and 'estrella volcanera' (Panama) for the volcano hummingbird and 'anteburro' (Costa Rica) for the tapir; 'venado cola blanca' is the wording of Ley 7497 and the Presidencia page.

unverified.claim: Elevation range and annual rainfall of the Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve (the plate assumes 1,400–1,600 m)
unverified.reason: The fetched Wikipedia article on the reserve does not state them; the reserve's own website was not fetched. The plate's band falls within the species-wide elevation ranges recorded for the quetzal and the mountain-gem, so the fit judgements do not depend on it.

unverified.claim: Gaceta publication date of Ley N.° 7497 (this project's research/country.json cites a MEP document giving 8 June 1995)
unverified.reason: The FAOLEX text gives the Assembly approval (24 April 1995) and signing (2 May 1995) dates but no Gaceta issue or date; the UNEP/FAOLEX record page that might state it failed to load (client error).

unverified.claim: Which white-tailed deer subspecies occurs in Costa Rica, and Costa Rican body measurements
unverified.reason: Spanish Wikipedia lists O. v. truei for 'Centroamérica' and O. v. chiriquensis for Panama without naming Costa Rica; the ACG page gives no measurements. The 60 kg ceiling is Spanish Wikipedia's statement about tropical deer in general.

unverified.claim: Presence of the white-tailed deer in Santa Rosa National Park as stated by the park's own documentation
unverified.reason: The ACG's deer page says the Guanacaste savannas, 'especialmente el Parque Nacional de Santa Rosa', have been its home, but the fetched Wikipedia article on Santa Rosa does not list the deer; the 1998 Revista de Biología Tropical study worked at La Emilia farm and Palo Verde, not Santa Rosa.

unverified.claim: Great blue heron: which subspecies reaches Costa Rica, its Costa Rican elevation range, and whether another heron species is 'more typical' of Tortuguero's canals
unverified.reason: No fetched page addresses the subspecies or elevation; the Tortuguero article names 'great blue herons' but no other heron species, so no comparison could be sourced. The seasonality (mainly October–April) is an interpretation of GBIF month counts for Limón province.

unverified.claim: A hummingbird species list for Irazú Volcano National Park (e.g. an eBird hotspot) confirming the volcano hummingbird at 2,800–3,400 m
unverified.reason: Two eBird region URLs found by search turned out to be other hotspots (Cordoncillo de Volcán, Puntarenas; Volcán Cosigüina, Nicaragua) and were not used. The Irazú fit rests on Wikipedia's subspecies range (Irazú and Turrialba) and on 3 GBIF records with elevation 2,800–3,400 m in Cartago.

unverified.claim: Which purple-throated mountain-gem subspecies occurs at Monteverde (Cordillera de Tilarán)
unverified.reason: Wikipedia names the Cordillera de Guanacaste for pectoralis and the Cordillera Central for the nominate, but not Tilarán.

unverified.claim: Plumage match of the green-and-blue hummingbird drawn on the Monteverde plate to the green-crowned brilliant or violet sabrewing
unverified.reason: Both species are on the eBird reserve list, but no page describing their plumage was fetched; the match is suggested, not asserted.

unverified.claim: Presence of Morpho helenor inside the Monteverde reserve, Corcovado and Tortuguero specifically
unverified.reason: GBIF evidence is at national (elevation band 1,300–1,700 m) or province level (Puntarenas 713, Limón 302 records); the Corcovado article counts 220 butterfly species without naming Morpho, and the Tortuguero and Monteverde articles do not mention butterfly species. Which Morpho species occur at Monteverde itself: nationally at 1,300–1,700 m GBIF lists M. helenor (22 records, plus 2 as M. peleides) and M. theseus justitiae (13).

unverified.claim: Altitudinal range of the clay-colored thrush in Costa Rica (the Stiles & Skutch-type upper limit) and its regular presence on the slopes of Irazú at 2,000–3,000 m
unverified.reason: Cornell's Neotropical Birds, English Wikipedia and the York University Las Nubes page (fetched in an earlier task) give no elevation; GBIF holds only 5 Costa Rican records with elevation data between 2,000 and 3,000 m (3 Pérez Zeledón, 1 Cartago, 1 San José). Recorded as uncertain; the plate should keep the bird on the farmed middle slopes.

unverified.claim: Caribbean-side scarlet macaw reintroductions (e.g. Sarapiquí) that could make a Tortuguero sighting plausible
unverified.reason: Spanish Wikipedia names release sites only on the Pacific side (Curú, Isla Tiskita, central Pacific) and the Tortuguero article names only the great green macaw; no page on Caribbean releases was found within budget.

unverified.claim: GBIF national occurrence totals for the six new species
unverified.reason: Not fetched, to stay within the fetch budget; presence in Costa Rica rests on eBird, GBIF province/elevation counts and the cited articles instead.

unverified.claim: Full verbatim IUCN assessor list and spelling for the tapir assessment
unverified.reason: The GBIF distributions record was read through the fetch tool, which rendered the first author as 'Garcìa'; recorded as 'García' with the full list as returned.

unverified.claim: Monteverde reserve altitude range (often given as roughly 1,400–1,800 m) and its exact position astride the continental divide.
unverified.reason: The CCT management plan and the two Ambientico articles give no altitude range; they only place the reserve in the Cordillera de Tilarán with rivers draining to both the Pacific (Guacimal) and the Caribbean (Peñas Blancas, Chiquito, Caño Negro). Spanish Wikipedia's reserve page returned url_not_found. Only the town's elevation (~1,330–1,400 m, English Wikipedia) is sourced.

unverified.claim: Monteverde reserve has six life zones.
unverified.reason: English Wikipedia says six (citing a tourism site); the CCT's 2025 management plan says the reserve protects four cloud-forest life zones. Sources conflict, so no count is given in the facts.

unverified.claim: Hanging bridges / Sky Walk / Selvatura at Monteverde.
unverified.reason: No fetched page (CCT, IUCN, Ambientico, Wikipedia Monteverde) describes them; private attractions outside the reserve were not researched.

unverified.claim: Children's Eternal Rainforest founded in 1987.
unverified.reason: The Monteverde Conservation League's page says only 'a campaign by a small group of Swedish students in the late 1980s'; no fetched page gives 1987.

unverified.claim: Golden toad last seen in 1989.
unverified.reason: Only English Wikipedia (uncited) gives 1989; Méndez & Pounds (2017) confirm the species was described in 1966, is endemic to Monteverde and its local population went extinct, without a date.

unverified.claim: Tenorio Volcano National Park area (12,900 ha / 129 km² vs '18,402.51 ha') and founding year (1976 vs 1995).
unverified.reason: sinac.go.cr's Tenorio page is robots-blocked; English and Spanish Wikipedia disagree and neither cites an official source for the area.

unverified.claim: Río Celeste daily visitor cap.
unverified.reason: No fetched page states a numerical cap for Tenorio Volcano National Park.

unverified.claim: Irazú is 'the highest active volcano' in Costa Rica and the lake's disappearance in a specific recent year (2010 or 2012).
unverified.reason: SINAC says 'el volcán más alto de Costa Rica' (highest, without 'active'); the GVP lists the last known eruption as 1977 and treats the 1994 event as possibly a landslide. The 2011 UCR paper lists dry years up to 1990 and Teletica (Jan 2020) says the lake was drying 'again' without giving the previous date. The decree number enlarging the park was read as '26945-MINAE of 22 August 1988' and may contain a transcription error.

unverified.claim: Painted oxcarts of Sarchí: specific history (Joaquín Chaverri's 1903 workshop, the giant oxcart, Eloy Alfaro factory).
unverified.reason: Only La Nación 2005 ('Sarchí es considerada la cuna de la artesanía en madera de las carretas') and the UNESCO description of the painting tradition were fetched; no page on Sarchí's workshops was read.

unverified.claim: The ACG's current total area as a single figure (147,000 ha UNESCO property; 120,000 + 70,000 ha per the ACG's 1997 page; ~169,000 ha per GDFCF).
unverified.reason: Figures refer to different dates and boundaries (World Heritage property vs the whole conservation area); SINAC's ACG page gives no area.

unverified.claim: Manuel Antonio is 'the smallest national park in Costa Rica' and its original 1972 area of 682–683 ha.
unverified.reason: Wikipedia says only 'one of the smaller'; the ICT page gives both 683 ha and 1,953 ha without explanation. SINAC's Manuel Antonio page was not fetched.

unverified.claim: Manuel Antonio's weekly closing day (Monday vs Tuesday).
unverified.reason: ICT says open 'Tuesday to Sunday'; Wikipedia says closed Tuesdays.

unverified.claim: Original National Geographic article calling Corcovado 'the most biologically intense place on Earth'.
unverified.reason: Teletica (2023) and Meteored (2024) attribute the phrase to National Geographic without citing an article; the English Wikipedia article does not contain the phrase; no nationalgeographic.com page with it was found by search.

unverified.claim: Corcovado holds 'the largest remaining Pacific lowland rainforest in Central America' and is a tapir 'stronghold'.
unverified.reason: Wikipedia's version ('the largest primary forest on the American Pacific coastline') is uncited; Baird's tapir is listed only as an endangered resident; no population figures were fetched.

unverified.claim: Tortuguero's canals were partly dug by hand or dredged (1960s–70s) to link natural lagoons.
unverified.reason: Neither the SINAC/ACTo brochure, ICT nor Wikipedia says which canals are artificial or when they were built; the brochure only names six caños.

unverified.claim: Tortuguero rainfall as a measured average (5,000–6,000 mm).
unverified.reason: Only Wikipedia's 'up to 250 inches (6,400 mm)' (secondary sources) was fetched; no IMN or SINAC rainfall figure.

unverified.claim: Tortuguero established 1975 (Wikipedia infobox) vs declared 24 September 1970 (ICT, STC).
unverified.reason: The 1975 date is probably the ratifying law, but no fetched page explains the two dates; the JSON uses 1970.

unverified.claim: routeFacts: width of Costa Rica between the oceans (narrowest/widest) and road distances San José–Puntarenas / San José–Limón.
unverified.reason: Neither the English nor the Spanish Wikipedia geography article gives the width or the road distances (both were fetched and checked); the fetch budget did not allow further searches, so the array was omitted.

unverified.claim: The exact Smithsonian GVP eruption table for Irazú (start/stop dates and VEI for each of the ~23 historical eruptions) and the basis for its 'Last Known Eruption 1977 CE' entry.
unverified.reason: The GVP page text read by WebFetch (107,085 characters) contained the description and bulletin reports but not the eruption table; the summary table's 1977 entry conflicts with the RSN, SINAC and Wikipedia, which treat 8 December 1994 as the last (phreatic) eruption. Recorded as approximate.

unverified.claim: Seven people killed by ejected material at the crater rim in 1964.
unverified.reason: Stated only by the Tico Times (2016) without a source; not found in Waldron, Murata et al., the RSN, SINAC or the GVP bulletin. Left out of the timeline.

unverified.claim: The CNE's official definition of its alert levels (verde, amarilla, naranja, roja) and the text of Ley 8488.
unverified.reason: cne.go.cr returned a client error and pgrweb is blocked for automated fetching (earlier tasks); the levels are described from El Mundo CR (2015), which lists only green, yellow and red, and Delfino (2025), which shows orange in use.

unverified.claim: A published Irazú volcanic hazard map (zonation of ash fall and lahars) from the RSN, CNE or Alvarado et al.
unverified.reason: No hazard map page was fetched; Clark et al. (2006) could only be read as a bibliographic record. Ash-dispersal statements rest on Waldron (1967), Murata et al. (1966), Alvarado & Schmincke (2013) and the RSN's one-line hazard list; lahar statements on Waldron and the Pavanelli EGU 2007 abstracts.

unverified.claim: Current (2026) OVSICORI activity level for Irazú on its 0–5 scale and the current state of the crater lake.
unverified.reason: The OVSICORI Irazú page failed to load and volcanodiscovery.com (which mirrors OVSICORI updates) returned a client error. The latest official status read is the RSN's March 2015 'semáforo verde, fase 2'; the latest OVSICORI statement read is Protti's September 2026 interview (no reactivation). Lake status: dry in 2014–2016 (RSN 2015, Tico Times 2016), back 2017, dry 2020 (Spanish Wikipedia, unsourced).

unverified.claim: Exact date of the 2020 summit landslide (26 vs 28 August 2020).
unverified.reason: Two La Nación reports citing OVSICORI seismographs and the CNE–OVSICORI report say 26 August 2020 (4:02 a.m.); Spanish Wikipedia says 28 August. The JSON uses 26 August.

unverified.claim: Exact death toll of the 9 December 1963 Reventado flow (15, 20 or 'more than 20') and the number of homes destroyed (300, 'more than 300', 400).
unverified.reason: Sources disagree; the JSON gives 'about 20' with the range, citing Waldron (>20, >300 homes), Pavanelli et al. (20), La Teja/Barquero (>15 dead, ~300 homes) and Wikipedia (20 dead, >400 homes overall).

unverified.claim: That Irazú's 1963–65 ash closed or disrupted San José's airport.
unverified.reason: No fetched source mentions aviation in 1963–65; the airport-closure clause in 'whatIf' rests on the Turrialba precedent of 12 March 2015 documented by the RSN.

unverified.claim: A SINAC rule stating when Parque Nacional Volcán Irazú closes for volcanic activity.
unverified.reason: SINAC's park page states no such rule; closures were documented case by case (Prusia trails after the 2020 landslide; CNE red alert prohibiting entry at Poás in 2025).

unverified.claim: Exact date, place, quantities and organisers of the 2003 gallo pinto cook-offs between Costa Rica and Nicaragua, and whether Guinness certified either
unverified.reason: English Wikipedia gives 2003, ~1,000 lb (Costa Rica) and 1,200 lb (Nicaragua) with no locations; The Tico Times (2004) only confirms that Costa Rica lost to Nicaragua in 2003; no Guinness page or contemporary report was fetched.

unverified.claim: When gallo pinto originated
unverified.reason: Fetched sources disagree: c. 1870–1875 in rural households (Rojas, Revista Herencia 2008); 19th-century Afro-Caribbean railroad workers (Vega Jiménez 2012 abstract); 1930s San José per the Costa Rican popular account reported by English Wikipedia; Jamaican banana-plantation workers per Wikipedia's 'Rice and peas'. Recorded as a dispute.

unverified.claim: Etymology of 'gallo pinto'
unverified.reason: Spanish Wikipedia says the origin of the name has not been clarified; the 2008 UCR article offers the bean-colour/speckled-rooster explanation; no documentary evidence was fetched.

unverified.claim: That gallo pinto is officially a 'national dish' of Costa Rica
unverified.reason: Only Wikipedia says both countries consider it a national dish; no Costa Rican law or decree naming a national dish was found.

unverified.claim: Origin of the name 'casado'
unverified.reason: All explanations (workers asking to be served 'como al hombre casado'; the components being 'married') are reported by La Nación and Wikipedia as stories attributed to Marjorie Ross or unnamed tradition; none is documented. Recorded as folklore.

unverified.claim: That the casado 'surgió en la época colonial'
unverified.reason: Stated by Teletica (2025) citing the website RecetasCostaRica.com; no academic or institutional source fetched supports a colonial origin, and La Nación places its consolidation in the 1960s.

unverified.claim: Date of the tamal's origin in Mesoamerica
unverified.reason: Sedó's UCR document cites archaeological claims of about 100 BC (San Bartolo murals) and elsewhere says 'más de tres mil años'; the two figures conflict and neither primary archaeological source was fetched.

unverified.claim: That plantain leaves replaced corn husks through African influence
unverified.reason: Sedó (UCR) presents this as a possibility ('posiblemente'), not a finding.

unverified.claim: Boiled versus steamed tamal
unverified.reason: The UCR source describes immersion in hot water for modern plantain-leaf tamales and steaming for the historical corn-husk tamal; English Wikipedia says the modern tamal is steamed. Recorded with the UCR version first and the conflict noted.

unverified.claim: Olla de carne as a specifically Sunday dish
unverified.reason: Spanish Wikipedia says 'fines de semana' (weekends); Teletica's 2022 Guápiles event cooked it on a Sunday; no fetched Costa Rican institutional or press source states a Sunday tradition in so many words.

unverified.claim: Olla de carne 'prepared for more than 100 years', associated with Cartago, and 'a tropicalised version of the Jewish adafina'
unverified.reason: The first is Spanish Wikipedia without a cited source; the Cartago and adafina claims come from Teletica (2025) citing the website Ticopedia.com; no academic or institutional source fetched supports them.

unverified.claim: Record for the most people eating olla de carne (600, at a supermarket event)
unverified.reason: Spanish Wikipedia statement with no date, place or source; Teletica's 2022 Guápiles 'olla más grande' cites no record-keeping body.

unverified.claim: Type of bean in Limón rice and beans
unverified.reason: Spanish Wikipedia's cuisine article and Teletica's 2024 recipe say red beans; Spanish Wikipedia's gallo pinto article says gongo/gandul (pigeon peas) with habanero; Teletica's 2026 report and the ICT mini-guide say only 'frijoles'.

unverified.claim: 'Chicken caribeño' as the standard accompaniment
unverified.reason: The ICT mini-guide says 'pollo en salsa' or fried fish; CRHoy says 'rice and beans con pollo' dominates in the capital while Limón's traditional version uses oxtail; no fetched source uses the term 'pollo caribeño' for the pairing.

unverified.claim: Direct descent of Limón rice and beans from Jamaican rice and peas
unverified.reason: Stated only by English Wikipedia ('Rice and peas'); the UNA article (Hutchinson Miller 2020) discusses Jamaican migration and identity but does not use the term 'rice and peas'.

unverified.claim: Absence of any heritage declaration for the five dishes
unverified.reason: Negative finding based on La Nación's 2026 list, Wikipedia's list, the patrimonio.go.cr home page and press coverage of MCJ cuisine programmes; sicultura.go.cr and mcj.go.cr blocked fetching and no official registry of declarations was obtained.

unverified.claim: Established Chinese names for the five dishes
unverified.reason: No fetched source gives one; the zh values are transliterations or descriptive names.

unverified.claim: Costa Rica has '112 volcanic structures' (or 'about 200 volcanoes').
unverified.reason: No fetched OVSICORI, RSN or peer-reviewed page gives such a total; Avard et al. (2021) count ten volcanic complexes and five historically active volcanoes, and Spanish Wikipedia's 'cerca de 200 volcanes' is unsourced. OVSICORI's volcano list page returned a server error.

unverified.claim: Exact current number of national parks (28, 29, 30, 31 or 32).
unverified.reason: sinac.go.cr blocks automated fetching; the only official count read is 28 (SINAC, 2014). Press and Wikipedia disagree (29–32).

unverified.claim: Current official bird list as published by the Unión de Ornitólogos / Asociación Ornitológica de Costa Rica on its own site or in Zeledonia.
unverified.reason: uniondeornitologos.com now shows only a domain-for-sale notice and repositorio.una.ac.cr rejected the requests (bot filter). The 942-species figure comes from a copy of the October 2025 official list hosted by a tour operator.

unverified.claim: '0.03 % of the Earth's surface' as a fraction of the whole planet.
unverified.reason: Arithmetically 51,180 km² is 0.034 % of the Earth's land area (~148.9 million km²) but only 0.010 % of its total surface (~510 million km²); the official reports say 'superficie terrestre' (land), and the site should too.

unverified.claim: A single current total for vascular plant species (e.g. 'about 10,000' or '11,000').
unverified.reason: The only fetched total is 11,467 known plant species from 2008 (SINAC, 2009); no newer official or Missouri Botanical Garden/Manual de Plantas de Costa Rica figure was obtained.

unverified.claim: Number of diurnal butterfly species (≈ 1,500) and of Lepidoptera overall (12,000–14,000).
unverified.reason: Only press sources (El Mundo CR 2019; La Nación 2007 quoting INBio) were fetched; no checklist or national report gives a butterfly total.

unverified.claim: Pacific coastline length (1,016 km vs 1,254 km) and total coastline (1,228 vs 1,290 km).
unverified.reason: Lengths depend on measurement scale; the 1,016 km figure was only found on Wikipedia, whereas a UCR article cites MINAE-PNUMA (2002) for 1,254 km. No IGN page with coastline lengths was fetched.

unverified.claim: Lake Arenal area from an ICE page (85–88 km²).
unverified.reason: The 87 km² figure comes from La Nación's 2019 report on the ICE complex, not from an ICE page.

unverified.claim: Forest cover minimum in the 1980s (21 % in 1987 per FONAFIFO vs ~26 % often quoted vs 40 % in 1986 per Sánchez 2015).
unverified.reason: Different mapping methods and forest definitions; FONAFIFO's own slide gives 21 % (1987), while a 2023 column citing Sánchez (2015) says cover never fell below 40 %. The 26 % figure was not found in any fetched source.

unverified.claim: Costa Rica has exactly 12 Holdridge life zones.
unverified.reason: Supported by a TEC conference paper (citing the CCT map) and Kohlmann et al. 2010, but a vocational text lists 17 units including transitions and an EGU 2019 abstract uses 11; the CCT map itself was not fetched.
